newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tiananmen impact slight for HK business 8 years on.
newsitem.headline: Tiananmen impact slight for HK business 8 years on.

text.p: The 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing shook investors and sparked turmoil over Hong Kong's return to China, but just weeks before the change of flag the territory's business mood is jubilant, analysts said on Wednesday.

"At the time (Tiananmen) happened it was devastating for everyone. The local Chinese, the overseas investors, were really affected and it had a major impact on all manners and forms of sentiment in this market," Andrew Fernow, director of research at Vickers Ballas, told Reuters.
"It took a while for that to subside. I think it did subside, however, because the economic argument was too great."
On June 4, 1989 the People's Liberation Army sent tanks and troops into Tiananmen Square to crush a student-led pro-democracy campaign, with heavy loss of life.

Hong Kong's blue chip Hang Seng Index plummeted 22 percent the following day to 2,093.61 points and the property market tumbled as Hong Kong people fled to seek residency elsewhere. Foreign investment, which had been pouring into China at the time, slowed down tremendously with companies refusing to invest on the mainland.

"People here were very shaken and a lot of old-time investors and local people basically said 'I don't want any part of this. I am out of here'," said Peter Churchouse, regional strategist at Morgan Stanley.
But eight years on, the Hang Seng Index is forging into record territory, driven by optimism that the change in sovereignty on July 1 will be smooth and that China's economic growth will power ahead.
The blue chip index closed at 14,831.58 points on Wednesday after hitting an all-time high of 15,020.96 on Tuesday.

But the blue chip performance has paled in relation to China-related stocks which have been the main investment theme this year. Residential property prices are also booming, with a rise of about 30 percent last year and another 20 to 30 percent increase expected this year. "People have taken a long hard look at China and Hong Kong over the last eight years to the day and have reassessed the situation," said Michael Green, an analyst at Salomon Brothers.
"China has come a long way in that time and Hong Kong has come a long way in that time.

"Confidence has returned and has been boosted even further by the fact that China showed potential to fall apart in 1989 and has defied all the sceptics by coming out very strongly and continuing the reform process."
China's economy is now expected to grow at a pace of nine to 10 percent over the next several years. Inflation is under control and standards of living have improved.
"Now China has its foot on the accelerator pedal. It has loosened credit and the economy is picking up," said Churchouse.
"There is a load of stuff that is quite positive and an increase in liquidity fund flows coming into Hong Kong. China is now in favour."
Analysts said investors were cautiously optimistic that Beijing had learnt from the past and would not treat social unrest in Hong Kong as it had done on the mainland.
Thousands of people were expected to gather in a Hong Kong park on Wednesday night for an annual candlelit vigil to mark the anniversary of the Tiananmen crackdown and to honour its dead.
"The rally itself is being used as a way to test the Beijing authorities' resolve with regard to allowing freedom of expression in Hong Kong in the future," said one analyst.
